title: The doctrine that broke Parliament's own rule
subtitle: Supremacy of EU law, and how a UK court came to disapply an Act of Parliament
objectives: Explain the CJEU's doctrine that EU law forms an autonomous legal order supreme over inconsistent national law, including later Acts of Parliament
Trace how section 2(4) of the European Communities Act 1972 gave that doctrine domestic effect in UK courts
State the significance of Factortame (No 2) as the moment a UK court disapplied a UK statute, and explain why this does not describe the UK's current constitutional position

leadingAuthorities.role: Establishes EU law as an autonomous legal order, supreme over inconsistent national law
Extends supremacy to override even national constitutional and fundamental-rights provisions

leadingAuthorities.citation: R v Secretary of State for Transport, ex p Factortame Ltd (No 2) [1991] 1 AC 603
leadingAuthorities.role: The House of Lords disapplies a provision of a UK Act of Parliament to give effect to EU law supremacy

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This lesson describes a doctrine the UK is no longer subject to — but it's the single most important piece of intellectual background for understanding parliamentary sovereignty as a live, contested idea. Where the profile shows application is ahead of understanding, this brief note appears: 'You can apply the mechanics — this lesson is about understanding why Factortame felt so constitutionally shocking at the time.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the reasoning here before. The test pool below leans towards scenario and 'why' questions rather than pure recall — expect to explain, not just name.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and don't rush Costa v ENEL — the whole doctrine, and everything that follows in this lesson, is built on the reasoning in that one case.

overview.hook: In 1964, a small unpaid electricity bill in northern Italy produced one of the most consequential judgments in the history of European law. By 1990, the same doctrine it created had reached the House of Lords and done something that, on paper, should have been constitutionally impossible: an English court told the Crown it could not enforce an Act of Parliament. This lesson tells that story in order — the quiet Italian case, the doctrine it built, and the moment it landed in London and nobody quite knew how to describe what had just happened.
overview.lawStatedNotice: The United Kingdom left the European Union on 31 January 2020, and EU law no longer takes supremacy over UK legislation. This lesson teaches the CJEU's supremacy doctrine and its domestic reception via the European Communities Act 1972 and Factortame as history — the intellectual and constitutional background that shaped UK law for nearly five decades, not as a description of the UK's current constitutional position. Costa v ENEL and Factortame are not current law in the UK; they remain important as the historical foundation that Public law's own treatment of parliamentary sovereignty (see Public law Lessons 2–3) builds on and reacts against. Law stated as at 1 September 2026.

parts.heading: A quiet revolution: Costa v ENEL
parts.voice: case-narrative — builds the drama before naming the doctrine
body: Flaminio Costa was an Italian lawyer and shareholder who refused to pay a 1,925 lire electricity bill — a few pence — to ENEL, Italy's newly nationalised electricity company. His objection wasn't really about the money. He argued the nationalisation law breached Italy's obligations under the EEC Treaty, and he wanted an Italian court to say so.

The Italian government's response looked, at the time, unanswerable: the nationalisation law was passed after Italy ratified the Treaty, and under ordinary principles of Italian constitutional law, a later statute simply overrides an earlier inconsistent one. The Treaty, on this view, was just another Italian law — junior to whatever Parliament passed next.

The Court of Justice disagreed, and did so in language that reached far beyond one Italian electricity bill. It held that in creating the Community, member states had 'limited their sovereign rights, albeit within limited fields' and created 'a body of law which binds both their nationals and themselves.' EU law, the Court said, formed its own autonomous legal order — one that could not be overridden by any later national legislation, however validly passed, because to allow that would let each state unpick the common project unilaterally, and 'the reciprocal obligations undertaken by states would no longer be certain but merely contingent.'

components.court: Court of Justice of the European Communities
components.factsShort: An Italian shareholder refused a small electricity bill, arguing Italy's nationalisation law breached the EEC Treaty; Italy argued the later statute simply overrode the earlier Treaty obligation.
components.ratioShort: EU law forms an autonomous legal order, integrated into member states' legal systems, which takes precedence over any inconsistent national law — including law passed after the Treaty.

expanded.facts: Costa, a shareholder in an electricity company nationalised by Italy in 1962, refused to pay a small bill and argued in the Milan magistrates' court that the nationalisation law conflicted with Italy's Treaty obligations. The Italian government argued the case was purely a matter of domestic law, since the later statute would prevail over the earlier Treaty under ordinary Italian constitutional principles.
expanded.judgmentExtract: By creating a Community of unlimited duration, having its own institutions, its own personality, its own legal capacity... the Member States have limited their sovereign rights, albeit within limited fields, and have thus created a body of law which binds both their nationals and themselves... The law stemming from the Treaty could not, because of its special and original nature, be overridden by domestic legal provisions, however framed, without being deprived of its character as Community law.
expanded.significance: This is the foundational statement of EU law supremacy — not written into the Treaty text itself, but constructed by the Court as a necessary condition for the Community project to function at all. Every later supremacy case, including Factortame, traces back to this reasoning.

interaction.prompt: On the Italian government's argument in Costa v ENEL, why should the later nationalisation statute have overridden the earlier Treaty obligation?
options: Because a later domestic statute displaces an earlier inconsistent one under ordinary Italian constitutional principles
Because the Treaty had never been properly ratified by Italy
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — this is the classic 'implied repeal' style argument: later law displaces earlier law. The Court's whole innovation was rejecting that this applied to Treaty obligations at all.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Italy's argument wasn't about ratification — it was a straightforward domestic-law point: under ordinary principles, a later statute overrides an earlier inconsistent one. The Court of Justice's achievement was refusing to let that principle apply to EU law.

parts.heading: No back door: Internationale Handelsgesellschaft
parts.voice: escalating — shows the doctrine being pushed to its hardest test
body: Costa v ENEL established supremacy over ordinary national statutes. Six years later, a German case tested something far more provocative: could EU law even override a member state's own constitutional protections — the kind of fundamental rights guarantees states treat as untouchable?

A German company challenged an EU agricultural regulation requiring an export deposit, arguing it breached principles protected by the Basic Law, Germany's constitution — including the constitutional right to pursue a trade freely and the principle of proportionality as understood in German constitutional law. If any national law should outrank EU law, surely it would be a state's own constitution.

The Court of Justice held otherwise. It ruled that the validity of an EU measure could only be judged against EU law itself — not against a member state's national law, 'whether it be a fundamental right or a constitutional principle.' Allowing national constitutions to override EU measures would fracture the uniform application of EU law across the Union. The Court did add a partial concession: fundamental rights formed part of the 'general principles' of EU law itself, protected within the EU legal order — but the source of that protection had to be EU law, not a national constitution reasserting authority over it.

components.definition: The core idea underlying supremacy: EU law does not derive its authority from, and is not subordinate to, the constitutional law of any individual member state — it forms a distinct legal system that member states agreed to create and be bound by.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that states why even national constitutional protections cannot override EU law.
interaction.passage: The validity of a Community measure or its effect within a Member State cannot be affected by allegations that it runs counter to either fundamental rights as formulated by the constitution of that State or the principles of a national constitutional structure. Recourse to the legal rules or concepts of national law in order to judge the validity of measures adopted by the institutions of the Community would have an adverse effect on the uniform application and efficacy of Community law.
interaction.ratioSentence: The validity of a Community measure or its effect within a Member State cannot be affected by allegations that it runs counter to either fundamental rights as formulated by the constitution of that State or the principles of a national constitutional structure.

parts.heading: How the UK let the doctrine in: s 2(4) ECA 1972
parts.voice: mechanical — walks through the statutory hinge carefully
body: Here is the puzzle Costa v ENEL and Internationale Handelsgesellschaft create for a dualist, parliamentary-sovereignty system like the UK's: EU law claims supremacy over even later domestic statutes, entirely on its own authority. But under classical UK constitutional theory, no treaty can bind Parliament, and no Parliament can bind its successors — a later Act always prevails over an earlier one, full stop.

The UK's answer, when it joined the Community in 1973, was the European Communities Act 1972 (ECA 1972) — a UK statute that gave domestic legal effect to EU law from the UK side. Section 2(1) made directly effective EU law automatically part of UK law without further enactment. Section 2(4) is the provision that did the real constitutional work: it required every UK enactment — passed before or after 1972 — to be construed and take effect 'subject to' directly effective EU law.

This is a genuinely clever piece of statutory engineering: it doesn't purport to bind future Parliaments in the abstract (which orthodox theory says is impossible) — it operates as an ordinary rule of statutory construction that later Acts are read subject to. On the ground, though, its practical effect was exactly what Costa v ENEL demanded: UK courts began reading Acts of Parliament as subordinate to EU law, without needing to abandon the formal theory of sovereignty outright.

components.text: ...any enactment passed or to be passed, other than one contained in this Part of this Act, shall be construed and have effect subject to the foregoing provisions of this section...
elements: Applies to any UK enactment — past or future
Requires that enactment to be 'construed and have effect subject to' directly effective EU law
Operates as a rule of statutory interpretation rather than a formal claim to bind future Parliaments

interaction.prompt: Why was s 2(4) ECA 1972 a constitutionally careful piece of drafting, rather than a straightforward claim that EU law simply overrides Parliament?
options: Because it required every UK court to refer supremacy questions to the CJEU before applying it

Because it operates as a rule of statutory construction — later Acts are read 'subject to' EU law — rather than an explicit claim to bind future Parliaments, which orthodox sovereignty theory says is impossible
Because it only applied to devolved legislatures, not to Westminster
interaction.trapExplanation: The clever part of s 2(4) is precisely that it avoids the impossible move (a Parliament binding its successors). It works through construction — telling courts how to read later Acts — which is compatible with orthodox sovereignty theory even though its practical effect achieves what supremacy demanded.

parts.heading: The Factortame shock
parts.voice: dramatic narrative — told as the constitutional crisis it felt like at the time
body: By the late 1980s, Spanish fishing companies had begun registering their vessels as British to fish against the UK's EU quota — a practice known as 'quota hopping'. Parliament responded with the Merchant Shipping Act 1988, which imposed nationality and residence requirements that effectively stripped these vessels of their British registration, cutting off their access to UK quota.

Factortame Ltd, a company affected by the Act, challenged it as contrary to EU law on freedom of establishment and non-discrimination on grounds of nationality — and applied for an interim injunction disapplying the Act while the substantive question went to the CJEU for a preliminary ruling. This raised a genuinely unprecedented question: could a UK court grant an interim injunction against the Crown, suspending an Act of Parliament, before any court had even decided the Act was unlawful?

Under orthodox UK constitutional theory, the answer looked obviously no — courts had no power to injunct the Crown, and certainly no power to suspend a validly passed statute on a merely provisional basis. The House of Lords referred the question to the CJEU, which held that a national court, faced with a conflict between EU law and national law, must set aside any rule of national law — including a rule preventing interim relief against the Crown — that would prevent EU law rights from being effectively protected.

When the case returned, the House of Lords in Factortame (No 2) granted the injunction, disapplying the relevant provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act 1988. Lord Bridge was explicit that this followed necessarily from what Parliament itself had done in 1972: by enacting the ECA 1972, Parliament had 'voluntarily accepted' that EU law should take priority over inconsistent national law — so there was, in his words, 'nothing in any way novel' in an English court giving effect to a limitation Parliament had itself created. Whatever the formal framing, the practical effect stunned much of the legal establishment: for the first time, an English court had suspended the operation of a UK Act of Parliament.

components.caseName: R v Secretary of State for Transport, ex p Factortame Ltd (No 2)
components.factsShort: Spanish fishing companies challenged registration requirements in the Merchant Shipping Act 1988 as contrary to EU law and sought an interim injunction suspending the Act pending a CJEU ruling.
components.ratioShort: A UK court must, where necessary to protect directly effective EU law rights, disapply an inconsistent provision of a UK Act of Parliament — including by granting interim relief against the Crown.

expanded.facts: The Merchant Shipping Act 1988 imposed nationality and residence conditions that stripped Spanish-owned vessels of British registration, cutting off their access to UK fishing quota. Factortame argued the conditions breached EU law on freedom of establishment and non-discrimination, and sought interim relief suspending the Act while the CJEU ruled on the substantive question.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Bridge: 'If the supremacy... of Community law over the national law of member states was not always inherent in the EEC Treaty... it was certainly well established in the jurisprudence of the Court of Justice long before the United Kingdom joined the Community. Thus, whatever limitation of its sovereignty Parliament accepted when it enacted the European Communities Act 1972 was entirely voluntary... there is nothing in any way novel in according supremacy to rules of Community law.'
expanded.significance: Factortame (No 2) is the moment the supremacy doctrine from Costa v ENEL landed concretely in a UK court, disapplying a UK statute. Its constitutional framing matters: the House of Lords did not say Parliament had lost sovereignty — it said Parliament had exercised its sovereignty by choosing, in 1972, to subordinate later inconsistent statutes to EU law. That framing is exactly what made the domestic reception of supremacy possible without abandoning orthodox constitutional theory outright.

interaction.prompt: Which of these best captures how Lord Bridge framed the House of Lords' decision in Factortame (No 2), as against the alternative reading many commentators feared at the time?
interaction.scenarioA: Lord Bridge held that EU law simply overrides Parliament by its own inherent authority, regardless of anything Parliament itself had done — sovereignty had been lost outright.
interaction.scenarioB: Lord Bridge held that Parliament had voluntarily accepted this limitation by enacting the ECA 1972 in 1972 — so giving effect to EU law supremacy was an exercise of sovereignty, not a loss of it.
interaction.explanation: This is the crucial distinction. Lord Bridge deliberately framed the outcome as consistent with sovereignty: Parliament had chosen, through its own statute, to accept this limitation — which is why the decision didn't require UK courts to abandon orthodox constitutional theory, even though its practical effect (suspending a later Act) looked revolutionary.

parts.heading: Where this leaves the UK now
parts.voice: closing — deliberately steps back from the doctrine to place it in current constitutional context
body: It's worth being precise about what this lesson has, and hasn't, shown. Costa v ENEL and Internationale Handelsgesellschaft describe a doctrine the CJEU built for the EU's own legal order — one the UK accepted, through its own statute, for 47 years. Factortame (No 2) is the clearest domestic evidence of how completely that acceptance reshaped how UK courts treated Acts of Parliament in practice.

None of this describes the UK's constitutional position today. The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020; the European Communities Act 1972 was repealed by the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018, and EU law no longer takes supremacy over UK legislation. A UK court today cannot disapply an Act of Parliament on the basis that it conflicts with EU law, because the statutory hinge — s 2(4) ECA 1972 — that made that possible no longer exists.

What survives is the intellectual legacy. This history is exactly what Public law's own treatment of parliamentary sovereignty builds on and reacts against — the classical Diceyan account of an unlimited, unbound Parliament, and the question of whether and how that account was ever really compromised by EU membership, are questions this module's Costa-to-Factortame arc puts flesh on. When you study parliamentary sovereignty in Public law, you're studying a debate this lesson gave you the missing half of.

components.title: From Costa v ENEL to today
components.description: The chain of reasoning from EU-law supremacy to its UK reception and eventual removal.

nodes.label: Costa v ENEL (1964): EU law is an autonomous legal order, supreme over inconsistent national law
Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (1970): supremacy extends even over national constitutional protections
ECA 1972, s 2(4): UK statute construes all UK enactments 'subject to' directly effective EU law
Factortame (No 2) (1991): House of Lords disapplies a provision of a UK Act to give effect to EU law
European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 repeals the ECA 1972; EU law supremacy over UK legislation ends
Today: UK courts cannot disapply an Act of Parliament for conflict with EU law — the statutory hinge is gone

edges.label: UK absorbs the doctrine via statute

components.textAlternative: The doctrine runs: Costa v ENEL establishes EU law as supreme over national law; Internationale Handelsgesellschaft extends this even over national constitutions; the UK absorbed the doctrine domestically through s 2(4) ECA 1972; Factortame (No 2) shows a UK court giving concrete effect to it by disapplying an Act of Parliament; the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 then repealed the ECA 1972, ending EU law supremacy over UK legislation — which is the position today.

interaction.prompt: A UK court in 2026 is asked to disapply a provision of a UK Act of Parliament because it conflicts with a CJEU ruling handed down last year. Analyse whether the court can do this.

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a UK court can disapply a UK Act of Parliament on the basis of a post-exit CJEU ruling.
modelAnswer.rule: The statutory hinge that once required UK enactments to be construed subject to EU law — s 2(4) ECA 1972 — was repealed by the EUWA 2018. Post-exit CJEU rulings carry no domestic legal force in UK courts; only a limited, defined body of pre-exit retained/assimilated case law has any continuing domestic status, and even that is a matter of UK statute, not EU authority.
modelAnswer.application: Because the 2025 CJEU ruling postdates exit, it falls entirely outside any retained-case-law provision and has no domestic legal effect at all. Without a statutory hinge like the old s 2(4), there is no mechanism by which a UK court could treat any Act of Parliament as subordinate to it.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The court cannot disapply the Act. Factortame-style disapplication depended entirely on the ECA 1972's continued existence, which ended with EU exit.

testPool.prompt: Name the case in which the CJEU first held that EU law forms an autonomous legal order supreme over inconsistent national law.
In Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, could a member state's own constitutional fundamental-rights provisions override an inconsistent EU measure?
options: No — the CJEU held EU law could not be judged against national constitutional law
Yes — constitutional rights always prevail over EU measures

testPool.prompt: Which best describes the constitutional significance of s 2(4) ECA 1972?
options: It repealed the classical doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty outright
It required later UK enactments to be construed and take effect subject to directly effective EU law, giving domestic effect to EU supremacy without a formal claim to bind future Parliaments
It gave the CJEU direct appellate jurisdiction over UK courts
testPool.trapExplanation: s 2(4) never purported to repeal sovereignty as a doctrine — its cleverness was achieving supremacy's practical effect through ordinary statutory construction. The CJEU also never gained direct appellate jurisdiction over UK courts; the link was the preliminary reference procedure, not an appeal structure.

testPool.prompt: Put these events in the Factortame litigation in the correct order.
items: Merchant Shipping Act 1988 imposes nationality/residence requirements
Factortame seeks an interim injunction disapplying the Act
The House of Lords refers the interim-relief question to the CJEU
The House of Lords grants the injunction in Factortame (No 2)

testPool.prompt: In the extract below from Lord Bridge's speech in Factortame (No 2), highlight the sentence that frames the decision as consistent with parliamentary sovereignty rather than a loss of it.
testPool.passage: Some public comments on the decision of the Court of Justice made in the wake of the judgment in this case treated it as much political controversy as constitutional novelty. Thus, whatever limitation of its sovereignty Parliament accepted when it enacted the European Communities Act 1972 was entirely voluntary. Under the terms of the Act of 1972 it has always been clear that it was the duty of a United Kingdom court, when delivering final judgment, to override any rule of national law found to be in conflict with any directly enforceable rule of Community law.
testPool.ratioSentence: Thus, whatever limitation of its sovereignty Parliament accepted when it enacted the European Communities Act 1972 was entirely voluntary.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario correctly reflects the UK's current post-exit constitutional position, rather than the pre-exit Factortame position?
testPool.scenarioA: A UK court in 2026 refuses to disapply a UK Act of Parliament despite an argument that it conflicts with a recent CJEU ruling, because no statutory mechanism gives that ruling domestic force.
testPool.scenarioB: A UK court in 1995 disapplies a provision of a UK Act because it conflicts with directly effective EU law, relying on s 2(4) ECA 1972.
testPool.explanation: A reflects today's position: with s 2(4) ECA 1972 repealed, there is no mechanism for a UK court to subordinate an Act of Parliament to EU law, whether old or new. B correctly describes the pre-exit position under Factortame, but that is history, not current law.

testPool.prompt: A student argues: 'Since Costa v ENEL is still cited in UK judgments, EU law supremacy must still partly apply in the UK.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Citation of a case in argument or judgment is not the same as that case stating current binding law — Costa v ENEL is cited as historical/comparative authority, not as a source of present UK obligation
Costa v ENEL has been overruled by the CJEU and can never be cited again
UK courts are legally prohibited from mentioning any EU case
testPool.explanation: Courts and commentators can and do cite historically important cases for context or comparative reasoning without those cases being current binding authority. Costa v ENEL remains intellectually important; it is not a source of present legal obligation on UK courts.

testPool.prompt: Which UK statute repealed the European Communities Act 1972, ending the statutory basis for EU law supremacy in the UK?
options: The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018
The Human Rights Act 1998

testPool.prompt: In 1993, two years after Factortame (No 2), a UK court is asked to disapply a different Act of Parliament because it conflicts with directly effective EU law on free movement of goods. Analyse whether the court can do this, applying the reasoning from Factortame (No 2).
factsToOrder: The case is decided in 1993, while the ECA 1972 (including s 2(4)) is in force
The conflicting UK Act postdates the ECA 1972
The EU law relied on is directly effective
Factortame (No 2) established that s 2(4) requires later Acts to be construed subject to directly effective EU law

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a UK court in 1993 can disapply a UK Act of Parliament that conflicts with directly effective EU law.
modelAnswer.rule: Under s 2(4) ECA 1972, as applied in Factortame (No 2), all UK enactments — including those passed after 1972 — must be construed and take effect subject to directly effective EU law.
modelAnswer.application: The conflicting Act postdates the ECA 1972 and the EU law relied on is directly effective, so s 2(4) requires the Act to be read subject to it. Factortame (No 2) is direct authority that a court may go so far as disapplying the conflicting provision to give effect to EU law.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Yes — applying Factortame (No 2), the court can and should disapply the conflicting provision of the Act, because s 2(4) ECA 1972 was in force and required this outcome.

testPool.prompt: Why is it inaccurate to say Factortame (No 2) shows that 'EU law overrode parliamentary sovereignty'?
options: Because the House of Lords never actually granted the injunction
Because Lord Bridge framed the outcome as Parliament's own voluntary exercise of sovereignty through the ECA 1972, not as an external doctrine defeating sovereignty
Because Factortame concerned devolved, not Westminster, legislation
testPool.trapExplanation: The injunction was granted, and Factortame concerned a Westminster Act (the Merchant Shipping Act 1988), not devolved legislation. The precise and examinable point is the framing: Lord Bridge treated the 1972 Act as Parliament exercising, not losing, its sovereignty.

section 2(4) of the European Communities Act 1972
testPool.correctSpan: section 2(4) of the European Communities Act 1972
testPool.explanation: s 2(4) ECA 1972 was repealed by the EUWA 2018 — its reliance in this scenario is the clearest marker that this describes the pre-exit legal position, not today's.

testPool.prompt: Which case established supremacy over even a member state's own constitutional protections, going further than Costa v ENEL's original holding?
testPool.explanation: Internationale Handelsgesellschaft extended supremacy to override even national constitutional guarantees. Factortame (No 2) is the UK's domestic application of the doctrine, not the case that extended its scope at EU level.

testPool.prompt: Does this module's account of Costa v ENEL and Factortame describe the UK's constitutional position in 2026?
options: No — it is taught as historical and comparative background; EU law supremacy no longer applies in the UK
Yes — Factortame remains directly applicable law today

testPool.prompt: A Public law essay asks you to explain the historical challenge EU membership posed to Diceyan parliamentary sovereignty. Which of this lesson's cases is the single most directly relevant authority to cite for that specific challenge landing in a UK court?
options: Factortame (No 2) [1991] 1 AC 603
Internationale Handelsgesellschaft [1970] ECR 1125
testPool.explanation: Internationale Handelsgesellschaft is important CJEU doctrine, but it's Factortame (No 2) that shows the doctrine actually landing in a UK court and being reconciled with (or, on some readings, challenging) Diceyan sovereignty — making it the more directly relevant authority for a Public law essay on that specific point.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating pre-Brexit supremacy doctrine as if it still describes UK law today. Every scenario question is testing whether you can hold two things at once: the doctrine's historical mechanics, and the fact that its statutory hinge (s 2(4) ECA 1972) no longer exists.
